summary: Mobility is returning toward pre‑pandemic levels with an MF‑Index of 72, yet fuel‑saving outcomes remain far below expectations and high‑mobility sectors continue to pose economic and environmental risks. Targeted WFH incentives and accelerated public‑transport capacity are needed to sustain the recovery and improve equity.

signals.detail: Theoretical modelling predicts 35.7 M L/week saved, but the government recorded only 334 k L in the first week of the mandate – roughly 1% of the ceiling – indicating that current policies are not delivering meaningful fuel savings.
Daily PT trips total 1,235,713, about 86% of the pre‑pandemic daily average (≈1.43 M) and correspond to a ridership component of 72.7, showing solid recovery but still below the 2019 baseline.

Logistics, construction and retail & services have mobility scores above 90 and WFH rates under 10%, creating a high risk of fuel demand spikes, congestion and emissions as economic activity ramps up.
WFH adoption is uneven – 60% in public/GLC entities versus just 15% in retail – leading to unequal commuting burdens and limiting the broader social benefits of remote work policies.

Fuel prices remain elevated (RON95 RM4.67/L, diesel RM5.27/L) providing price pressure for a shift to public transport, yet ridership has not fully capitalised on this, suggesting modest progress toward a lasting modal shift.

recommendation: Introduce tiered WFH incentives to raise telecommuting in high‑mobility sectors to at least 30% by Q2 2027, pair them with a fuel‑rebate scheme for firms achieving the target, and allocate RM2 billion to expand PT capacity to lift daily ridership to 1.3 M by end‑2027, thereby improving equity and reducing fuel demand.
